newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbian opposition New Year rally draws huge crowd.
newsitem.headline: Serbian opposition New Year rally draws huge crowd.

text.p: Police kept a discreet distance as hundreds of thousands of Serbian opposition supporters jammed into central Belgrade on Monday for an Orthodox New Year's Eve rally.

"The police did their part, as if we're in power," student organiser Srdja Popovic said as final preparations were made for the rally in Republic Square expected to last until the early hours of the morning.

Initial estimates put the crowd at about 200,000 before the beginning of a programme which organisers said would include choral singing, rock music and video messages from Orthodox Patriarch Pavle and British actress Vanessa Redgrave and rock singer Sting.

Virtually no police were in sight as sound stages were assembled and video screens erected for the rally on the 57th straight day of protests against a decision by President Slobodan Milosevic's Socialist government to annul the results of municipal elections held on November 17.
The Zajedno (Together) coalition is demonstrating to press its claim to have won 14 of Serbia's 18 largest cities, including the capital Belgrade.

The students support the election demands and are demanding educational reforms, including the sacking of the university rector. They won a victory on Monday when senior academics, led by a prominent ruling socialist, backed protests against election fraud.

The Belgrade University governing board "supports the students' demands accepted by the Serbian deputy prime ministers and urges fulfilment of the commitments undertaken by them", said Rector Dragutin Velickovic, a Socialist Party appointee.
Two Serbian deputy prime ministers agreed on Saturday to student demands for recognition of opposition election victories, access to state media, and Velickovic's dismissal.
The board also said "students will not bear any consequences for taking part in the protests but must return to classes once their demands were fulfilled".
Serbian television said the justice ministry again told the municipal electoral commission in Nis, Serbia's second largest city, that the Zajedno coalition had won the municipal elections there.
The justice ministry warning reinforced a statement last week in which the government admitted for the first time that the opposition had won in Nis.
Earlier the opposition urged the army and police to quickly declare their position on alleged demands by powerful leftists that the eight-week-old protests be crushed.

"Top officials of the Socialist Party of Serbia (SPS) and the Yugoslav United Left (JUL) are demanding that the police use force to crush demonstrations in Serbia," the Zajedno coalition said in a statement.
Zajedno alleged that SPS and JUL were "obviously seeking to provoke large conflicts and impose an official state of emergency in Serbia".

Zajedno did not reveal the source of its information but respected independent media have reported that a hardline faction, concentrated in JUL, was pushing for drastic police action to get the protesters off the streets.
However, support for violent repression was believed to be weak in the army and not as strong in the security police as in similar situations earlier in Milosevic's decade-old rule.
At a recent meeting with Belgrade students, Yugoslav army chief General Momcilo Perisic said the military would stay neutral, tacitly backing the protesters.
Police have also exercised restraint except for random beatings meted out one night by plainclothes thugs.
The opposition previously drew hundreds of thousands of people to central Belgrade for demonstrations on the eve of Orthodox Christmas, celebrated on January 7.
